# ENUMERATION OF ONE-CYCLE SIGNED CHORD DIAGRAMS AND THEIR DUALS FOR OPTIMAL MORSE FLOWS ON CLOSED SURFACES A PREPRINT **Alexandr Prishlyak**
Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv, Ukraine
`prishlyak@knu.ua` October 15, 2026 **ABSTRACT** Optimal Morse vector fields on closed surfaces, i.e. fields with the minimal possible number of critical points (a single source and a single sink), are classified up to topological trajectory equivalence by one-cycle signed chord diagrams Kybalko et al. (2018).We recall this construction and the associated duality, which corresponds to reversing the direction of the flow, in a unified encoding in which both endpoints of a chord carry the same label, and we make it algorithmic. We give an explicit traversal procedure that detects one-cycle diagrams, a canonical form of an equivalence class under cyclic shifts, reversal and relabeling of chords, and a construction of the dual diagram. On this basis we describe an algorithm that enumerates all one-cycle signed chord diagrams with a given number of chords, both for orientable and for non-orientable surfaces, groups them into equivalence classes, pairs each class with its dual, and identifies the self-dual ones. The algorithm is implemented in Python and archived in Zenodo; its output is validated against the Harer–Zagier numbers in the orientable case and against orbit-size counts in both cases. We also note that, when a one-cycle diagram is read as a cellular embedding of a one-vertex graph, its dual diagram describes the embedding of the dual graph. **_Keywords_** Morse flow · topological classification · vector field · signed chord diagram · dual diagram · surface topology ### 1 Introduction The topological classification of dynamical systems is a foundational problem in geometric topology and the qualitative theory of differential equations. Structurally stable systems are of particular importance because their qualitative phase portraits remain invariant under small _C_1-perturbations of the vector field Peixoto (1959); Palis and de Melo (1982). On closed surfaces, such structurally stable flows are precisely the Morse–Smale vector fields Peixoto (1973); Oshemkov and Sharko (1998); Kibkalo and Yokoyama (2022). Gradient-like systems and Morse flows arise naturally as gradient fields of Morse functions with respect to suitable Riemannian metrics Smale (1960, 1961). According to Smale’s construction, an optimal Morse flow, that is, one with a single source and a single sink, specifies a polar Morse function once all saddle points are placed at the same critical level. In Fomenko’s topological classification of integrable Hamiltonian systems and of functions on surfaces Bolsinov and Fomenko (2004), such a structure is a simple atom with one input and one output, which corresponds to an edge of degree 2 in the associated Reeb (Kronrod– Reeb) graph Reeb (1946); Kronrod (1950); Kravchenko and Maksymenko (2019); Tereshchenko and Prishlyak (2024); Tereshchenko et al. (2025). The global topological structure of such flows is therefore encoded by one-cycle signed (marked) chord diagrams Kybalko et al. (2018). Fine topological invariants and combinatorial structures for flows and functions on surfaces have been developed in many settings. For closed two-dimensional manifolds, combinatorial schemes, three-color graphs, chord diagrams and _F_-atoms were used to classify optimal flows, simple Morse functions and functions with non-degenerate critical points

<tbc>Prishlyak (1997, 2000, 2002c); Kybalko et al. (2018); Prishlyak and Skochko (2016); Prishlyak and Loseva (2020). These methods were extended to surfaces with boundary and to non-compact surfaces, where complete classifications and deformation theories are available Prishlyak and Mischenko (2007); Hladysh and Pryshlyak (2016); Hladysh and Prishlyak (2017, 2019a,b); Prishlyak and Prus (2017); Prishlyak and Loseva (2019); Prishlyak and Prus (2020); Borodzik et al. (2016); Prishlyak and Ovtsynov (2026), and to flows on non-orientable surfaces such as the projective plane, the Möbius strip, the Klein bottle and Boy’s and Girl’s surfaces Prishlyak and Di Beo (2022); Prishlyak and Loseva (2023); Prishlyak and Stas (2025); Prishlyak and Butok (2025). In higher dimensions, topological invariants, handle decompositions, Heegaard diagrams and conjugacy classifications have been obtained for flows and functions on 3- and 4-manifolds Prishlyak (1998, 1999a,b, 2001a, 2002b, 2003a, 2001b,c, 2002a, 2003b, 2005, 2007); Prishlyak and Vyatchaninova (2013); Hatamian and Prishlyak (2020); Prishlyak et al. (2023a,b). Related work on codimension-one flows, bifurcations, closed 1-formsand collective dynamics can be found in Bilun and Prishlyak (2002); Prishlyak et al. (2021); Prishlyak and Ovtsynov (2025).

Chord diagrams, that is, perfect matchings of points on a circle, are also a classical object of enumerative combinatorics. The numbers of chord diagrams and of gluings of polygon sides into surfaces of given genus were studied by Harer and Zagier Harer and Zagier (1986), and an analogue of their formula for unicellular bicolored maps was obtained in Adrianov (1997). Counting chord diagrams of a given genus up to rotations was done by Cori and Marcus (1998), who in particular treated the maximal case, that is, diagrams of genus _g_ with 2_g_ chords; Krasko (2017) extended this count to the full dihedral group. The orientable one-cycle diagrams of the present paper are exactly these maximal diagrams. Enumeration of chord diagrams of other types, motivated by Vassiliev knot invariants, and of diagrams up to rotation and reflection is given in Stoimenow (2000); Khruzin (2000). Chord diagrams were further used as an invariant of functions on surfaces by Kadubovsky, who classified functions with one essentially critical point on oriented surfaces with boundary by means of color chord diagrams Kadubovsky and Klimchuk (2003), studied the realization and topological equivalence of functions with a single saddle point on oriented surfaces and counted non-equivalent functions for surfaces of prime-related genus Kadubovskyi (2006), and computed the numbers of non-equivalent minimal functions on closed oriented and non-orientable surfaces Kadubovskyi (2015). In a series of papers by Kadubovskyi and his co-authors, two-color chord diagrams with a prescribed number of faces are enumerated under the action of the cyclic and the dihedral groups, with explicit formulas and tables of values Kadubovskyi and Sypchuk (2020); Kadubovskyi et al. (2021). Our one-cycle diagrams belong to the same circle of enumeration problems, but we treat the orientable and the non-orientable case, all genera and the pairing with duals within a single algorithm.

The chord diagram construction for optimal flows and the duality that corresponds to time reversal are due to Kybalko et al. (2018). The aim of the present paper is to make this theory algorithmic. In contrast to the classical notation, in which the two endpoints of a chord carry different indices, each chord here receives one label \(i\in\{1,\dots,k\}\) that occurs twice along the circle, which gives a canonical chord code of length 2_k_. We recall the connection between one-cycle chord diagrams, Reeb graphs and embeddings of one-vertex graphs, and we give an explicit cycle-tracing procedure, a canonical form of an equivalence class, a construction of the dual diagram, and an enumeration algorithm for all one-cycle signed chord diagrams with a given number of chords. The algorithms are implemented in Python and archived together with visualization tools on Zenodo Prishlyak (2026a,b).

We describe an algorithm that, for given _g_, enumerates all one-cycle chord diagrams and identifies the pairs of dual diagrams, corresponding to the flows _X_ and -_X_, together with the self-dual diagrams, whose flows are equivalent to their reverses.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 collects the necessary facts on Morse-Smale flows, optimal Morse flows and topological equivalence. Section 3 introduces signed chord diagrams, the code with identical endpoint labels and the canonical form of an equivalence class. Section 4 recalls the construction of the chord diagram of an optimal flow and shows that it is a one-cycle diagram. Section 5 treats the chord cycle and the dual diagram, and Section 6 describes the enumeration algorithm, its implementation and the numerical results.

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 Morse-Smale and optimal Morse flows

We consider _C<sup>r</sup>_-smooth (\(r\ge 1\)) dynamical systems with continuous time (flows) on a smooth compact surface _M_. Let _X_ be a vector field generating the flow _X<sub>t</sub>_; the trajectory through \(x\in M\) is denoted by \(\varphi_t(x)=X_t(x)\).

**Definition 2.1.** Fixed (singular) points and closed trajectories are called the _critical elements_ of _X_.

**Definition 2.2.** A singular point _p_ of _X_ is _hyperbolic_ (non-degenerate) if the Jacobian matrix

\(\left(\frac{\partial X_i}{\partial x_j}(p)\right)_{i,j=1}^2,\) (1)

<tbc>written in local coordinates, has no eigenvalue with zero real part. A closed trajectory \(\gamma\) is _hyperbolic_ if the differential at \(p\in\gamma\) of the Poincaré return map has no eigenvalue of absolute value 1.

**Definition 2.3.** A point \(y\in M\) is an \(\omega\)-limit (\(\alpha\)-limit) point of \(x\in M\) if there is a sequence \(t_i\rightarrow+\infty\) (\(t_i\rightarrow-\infty\)) such that \(\varphi_{t_i}(x)\rightarrow y\). The set of all such points is the \(\omega\)-limit (\(\alpha\)-limit) set \(\omega(x)\) (\(\alpha(x)\)).

**Definition 2.4.** The _stable_ and _unstable manifolds_ of a critical element _c_ are

\(W^s(c)=\{x\in M|\omega(x)=c\},W^u(c)=\{x\in M|\alpha(x)=c\}.\)

For a singular point _p_ this means \(lim_{t\rightarrow+\infty}\varphi_t(x)=p\) and \(lim_{t\rightarrow-\infty}\varphi_t(x)=p\), respectively; in particular \(p\in W^s(p)\cap W^u(p)\).

**Definition 2.5.** A point \(p\in M\) is _wandering_ for _X_ if there are a neighborhood _V_ of _p_ and _T\>_0 such that \(X_t(V)\cap V=\emptyset\) for all |_t|\>T_; otherwise _p_ is _non-wandering_. The set of non-wandering points is denoted by \(\Sigma(X)\).

**Definition 2.6.** A vector field _X_ on a compact surface _M_ is a _Morse-Smale vector field_ if (1) _X_ has finitely many critical elements, all hyperbolic; (2) \(\Sigma(X)\) is the union of the critical elements; (3) the stable and unstable manifolds of critical elements intersect transversally.

Hyperbolic singular points of a flow on a surface are of three types: _sinks_, _saddles_ and _sources_. With the convention _X_=-grad_f_ for a Morse function _f_, they correspond to critical points of index 0, 1 and 2, respectively. Transversality excludes trajectories going from one saddle to another (saddle connections), since such a trajectory would lie in both _W<sup>u</sup>_ and _W<sup>s</sup>_ with the same tangent direction.

**Definition 2.7.** A Morse-Smale flow is a _Morse flow_ if it has no closed trajectories. A Morse flow on a closed surface _M_ is _optimal_ if it has the minimal number of singular points among all Morse flows on _M_.

**Theorem 2.8.** _Let M be a closed connected surface. Then:_

(_a)_ _a Morse flow on M is optimal if and only if it has exactly one sink and exactly one source;_<tbc>

_(b)_ _an optimal Morse flow has_ \(k=2-\chi(M)\) _saddles; thus k_=2_g if M is orientable of genus g, and k=h if M is non-orientable of genus h._

_Optimal Morse flows exist on every closed connected surface._

_Proof._ Let _a,b_, _k_ be the numbers of sources, sinks and saddles of a Morse flow. The sum of the indices of the singular points is \(\chi(M)\) (Poincaré-Hopf), and a source or sink has index +1, a saddle -1; hence \(a+b-k=\chi(M)\) and the total number of singular points is \(a+b+k=2(a+b)-\chi(M)\). Since \(\Sigma(X)\) is the finite set of singular points, \(\omega(x)\) is a single singular point _p_ for every _x_. Take _x_ outside the one-dimensional stable manifolds of the saddles and outside the singular points; then _p_ is not a saddle, and not a source (as _W<sup>s</sup>(p_)={_p_} for a source), hence a sink. So \(b\ge 1\), and by time reversal \(a\ge 1\). Therefore \(a+b\ge 2\) with equality exactly when _a=b_=1, which gives (a) and \(k=2-\chi(M)\). Existence is shown in Kybalko et al. (2018) (equivalently, via a Morse function with one maximum and one minimum).

## 2.2 Topological equivalence

**Definition 2.9.** Two vector fields _X,Y_ on _M_ are _topologically (trajectory) equivalent_, _X∼Y_ , if there is a homeomorphism \(h:M\rightarrow M\) that maps trajectories of _X_ onto trajectories of _Y_ and preserves the direction of motion along them. The homeomorphism _h_ is not required to preserve an orientation of _M_.

The time parametrization is ignored. The _inverse_ of _X_ is the field -_X_, with the same trajectories traversed in the opposite direction. In general \(X\unknown-X\), so the relation "_X_∼-_Y_" is a different, weaker condition; both occur in Section 5.

**Theorem 2.10.** _Let h be a topological equivalence of X and Y. Then p is a singular point of X iff h(p_) _is a singular point of Y ; a trajectory of X is closed iff its image is closed; and h maps the_ \(\alpha\)_-limit (_\(\omega\)_-limit) set of every trajectory onto the_ \(\alpha\)_-limit (_\(\omega\)_-limit) set of the image trajectory._

**Definition 2.11.** A vector field \(X\in\mathcal{X}^r(M)\), \(r\ge 1\), is _structurally stable_ if it has a neighborhood _U(X_) in the _C<sup>r</sup>_-topology such that _Y∼X_ for all \(Y\in U(X)\).

On closed surfaces the structurally stable fields are exactly the Morse-Smale fields Peixoto (1973); Oshemkov and Sharko (1998); Kibkalo and Yokoyama (2022); in particular, optimal Morse flows are structurally stable, and their classification up to ∼ is the object of this paper.

## 3 Signed Chord Diagrams and Canonical Encoding

We formalize chord diagrams using a unified endpoint labeling system suitable for algorithmization.

**Definition 3.1.** A _chord diagram D_ with _k_ chords consists of a boundary circle _S_<sup>1</sup>, 2_k_ distinct points on _S_<sup>1</sup>, and _k_ chords connecting these points in pairs (chords may cross when drawn in the disk).

In our encoding scheme:

• Each chord is assigned a unique identifier \(i\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\).<tbc>

• Both endpoints of chord _i_ are assigned the same integer label _i_.<tbc>

• Traversing _S_<sup>1</sup> counterclockwise from a fixed origin yields a sequence **c**=(_c_<sub>0</sub>_,c_<sub>1</sub>_,...,c_<sub>2_k_-1</sub>) of length 2_k_ in which each integer from 1 to _k_ appears exactly twice; positions are indexed by Z<sub>2_k_</sub>.

**Definition 3.2.** A code **c** is in _Restricted Growth String (RGS) canonical form_ if _c_<sub>0</sub>=1, and for every _m_ with \(1\le m<k\) the first occurrence of _m_ precedes the first occurrence of _m_+1. For an arbitrary sequence **w** in which every label occurs twice, its _RGS normalization_ relabels the chords in order of first occurrence.

The RGS codes of length 2_k_ are in bijection with the perfect matchings of 2_k_ points; there are (2_k_-1)!! of them.

**Definition 3.3.** A _signed chord diagram_ (or marked chord diagram) assigns a sign \(\sigma_i\in\{+1,-1\}\) to each chord \(i\in\{1,\dots,k\}\).

**Definition 3.4.** Two signed chord diagrams _D_<sub>1</sub>_,D_<sub>2</sub> are _isomorphic_ if one can be transformed into the other via a cyclic shift of the code and a relabeling of the chords (signs are carried along with their chords). They are _equivalent_ if they can additionally be related by a reversal (mirror reflection) of the boundary circle. We write \(D_1\simeq D_2\) for equivalence.

### 3.1 Canonical form of an equivalence class

Let G be the dihedral group of order 4_k_ generated by the cyclic shift and the reversal of the code. For \(g\in\mathcal{G}\) the diagram \(g\cdot D\) is obtained by applying _g_ to the code, taking the RGS normalization, and carrying the signs along with their chords (shifts and reversals do not change signs; relabeling permutes them). The _canonical form_ of _D_ is the lexicographic minimum

\(\mathrm{can}(D)=\mathrm{min}_{g\in\mathcal{G}}g\cdot D.\) (2)

Two signed diagrams are equivalent iff their canonical forms coincide. It is computed in _O(k_<sup>2</sup>) time (4_k_ images, each normalized in _O(k_)). If G is replaced by its cyclic subgroup of order 2_k_ (shifts only), the same procedure yields isomorphism classes. The orbit of _D_ consists of 4_k/_|Stab(_D_)| distinct normalized codes; the stabilizer is the group of symmetries of _D_.

## 4 Construction of a Chord Diagram from an Optimal Flow

The construction of a chord diagram from an optimal Morse flow follows Kybalko et al. (2018); we recall it here in the notation of Section 4.

Let _M_ be a closed connected surface (orientable or not) and _X_ an optimal Morse vector field on _M_, i.e. a Morse flow with a single source _x_<sub>0</sub>, a single sink _y_<sub>0</sub>, and _k_ saddle points _s_<sub>1</sub>_,...,s<sub>k</sub>_. By Theorem 2.8, the number of saddles is \(k=2-\chi(M)\), that is, _k_=2_g_ if _M_ is orientable of genus _g_ and _k_ equals the non-orientable genus otherwise.

**Neighborhood of the source.** Let _U(x_<sub>0</sub>) be a small closed disk around _x_<sub>0</sub> whose boundary \(\partial U(x_0)\cong S^1\) is transversal to the trajectories of _X_ leaving _x_<sub>0</sub>; each such trajectory meets \(\partial U(x_0)\) exactly once.

**Chords.** For each saddle _s<sub>i</sub>_, the set _W<sup>s</sup>(s<sub>i</sub>_)\\{_s<sub>i</sub>_} consists of two trajectories (separatrices) issuing from _x_<sub>0</sub> and entering _s<sub>i</sub>_. Hence <o>_W<sup>s</sup>(s<sub>i</sub>_)</o> meets \(\partial U(x_0)\) in exactly two points. Stable manifolds of distinct saddles are disjoint, so these _k_ pairs of points are pairwise disjoint on \(\partial U(x_0)\), which gives 2_k_ distinct points. Joining the two points of each pair by a chord inside the circle (the chords may cross each other in the picture) and labeling it by _i_ yields a chord diagram with _k_ chords.

**Signs.** Let _V<sub>i</sub>_ be a regular neighborhood of \(U(x_0)\cup\overline{W^s(s_i)}\), i.e. the disk _U(x_<sub>0</sub>) with one band attached along the two points of the chord _i_. If _V<sub>i</sub>_ is orientable (an annulus), put \(\sigma_i=+1\); if _V<sub>i</sub>_ is a Möbius band, put \(\sigma_i=-1\). (In terms of the marking, +1 corresponds to an unmarked and -1 to a marked chord.)

**Proposition 4.1.** _The signed chord diagram D<sub>X</sub> constructed above is a one-cycle diagram. Its chord cycle is the boundary of the basin of attraction of the sink y_<sub>0</sub>.

_Proof._ The set \(\Gamma=\{x_0\}\cup\bigcup_i\overline{W^s(s_i)}\) is a bouquet of _k_ circles embedded in _M_ (the loop number _i_ is formed by the two separatrices entering _si_). Every point of \(M\backslash\Gamma\) lies on a trajectory with \(\omega\)-limit _y_0, so \(M\backslash\Gamma\) is the basin of attraction of the sink, which is an open disk. Hence \(\Gamma\) is a cellular embedding with a single face, and the boundary of this face, read along \(\partial U(x_0)\) and the chords, is exactly the traversal (3) with the signs defined above. **Dependence on choices.** The diagram depends on the choice of the disk _U(x_0), of the initial point on \(\partial U(x_0)\), of the orientation of \(\partial U(x_0)\) (we do not fix an orientation of _M_), and of the numbering of the saddles. Changing them results, respectively, in an isotopy of the diagram, a cyclic shift of the code, a reversal, and a relabeling of the chords; the signs are unchanged by the first three operations and are carried along with their chords by the last one. Thus every optimal Morse flow on a closed surface induces a well-defined equivalence class of signed one-cycle chord diagrams (Section 3). Conversely, every equivalence class of one-cycle diagrams is realized by an optimal flow (Kybalko et al., 2018, Theorem 3). ## 5 Dual Chord Diagrams and Trajectory Cycles We formalize the dualization procedure (formerly termed inverse diagrams) under the identical-label code format. ### 5.1 Tracing the chord cycle Informally: start on a boundary arc between two chord endpoints and move counterclockwise; on reaching an endpoint of chord _i_, jump along the chord to its opposite endpoint; then continue along _S_1 in the same direction if \(\sigma_i=+1\), and in the reversed direction if \(\sigma_i=-1\); repeat until the starting arc is reached again in the same direction. Formally, for a position _p_ let \(\pi(p)\) be the position of the second endpoint of the chord _cp_. A _state_ is a pair \((p,\varepsilon)\) with \(p\in\mathbb{Z}_{2k}\) and \(\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}\): the walker stands at the point _p_ and is about to move along the boundary arc towards the neighbouring point \(p+\varepsilon\). One step is \((p,\varepsilon)\longmapsto\big(\pi(q),\varepsilon\sigma_{c_q}\big),q=p+\varepsilon,\) (3) where _q_ is called the _arrival point_. The tracing starts in the state (0,+1), i.e. on the arc right after the first element of the code, and stops when this state recurs. The arrival points _q_1_,...,qm_ define the _visit sequence_ **w**=(_c__q_1_,...,cqm_). **Algorithm 1** Tracing the chord cycle Require: code **c**, signs \(\sigma\)
\((p,\varepsilon)\leftarrow(0,+1)\); \(Q\leftarrow[]\triangleright\) list of arrival points
repeat
\(q\leftarrow(p+\varepsilon)mod2k\); append q to Q
\(\varepsilon\leftarrow\varepsilon\cdot\sigma_{c_q}\); \(p\leftarrow\pi(q)\)
until \((p,\varepsilon)=(0,+1)\)
return Q The map (3) is a permutation of the 4_k_ states, so the loop terminates in at most 4_k_ steps. **Definition 5.1.** A _chord cycle_ is the closed traversal path generated by (3). A diagram is a _one-cycle diagram_ if |_Q_|=2_k_ and every label 1_,...,k_ occurs exactly twice in **w**; equivalently, a single traversal covers all chords twice and all 2_k_ boundary arcs. For \(\sigma\equiv+1\) the cycle passes every chord once in each direction. For a chord with \(\sigma_i=-1\) both passes may arrive at the same endpoint, so the arrival points need not be pairwise distinct. For a one-vertex one-face map with _k_ edges the Euler characteristic is 2-_k_; hence one-cycle diagrams with all signs +1 exist only for _k_=2_g_ (orientable surface of genus _g_), and one-cycle diagrams with at least one sign -1 describe non-orientable surfaces of genus _k_. ### 5.2 Dual chord diagram Orient each chord _i_ from its endpoint _ai_ to its endpoint _bi_, where _ai\i_ are the positions of its endpoints in **c**. In the visit sequence **w** the label _i_ occurs twice, and each occurrence is an arrival either at _ai_ or at _bi_; the jump after an arrival at _ai_ runs along the chord in the positive direction, after an arrival at _bi_ in the negative one. To construct the _dual chord diagram D_∗ of a one-cycle diagram _D_:

1. Trace the chord cycle of _D_ and form the visit sequence **w** of length 2_k_.<tbc>

2. The dual code is the RGS normalization **c**<sup>∗</sup> of **w**; let \(\mu\) be the relabeling that sends the labels of _D_ to the labels of **c**<sup>∗</sup>.<tbc>

3. The sign \(\sigma_{\mu(i)}^*\) is +1 if the cycle runs along chord _i_ in opposite directions (the two arrivals are at different endpoints), and -1 if it runs along _i_ in the same direction (both arrivals at the same endpoint).<tbc>

4. Replace the result by its canonical form (2).

Since **w** depends on the base point and the direction of the tracing, the dual is a well-defined _equivalence class_.

**Lemma 5.2.** _If D is a one-cycle diagram, then D_<sup>∗</sup> _is a one-cycle diagram,_ \(D^{**}\simeq D\)_, D and D_<sup>∗</sup> _have the same (non- )orientable genus, and the class of D_<sup>∗</sup> _depends only on the class of D. Consequently, if N is the number of equivalence classes, K the number of unordered pairs_ {\[_D_\],\[_D_<sup>∗</sup>\]} _and s the number of self-dual classes, then s_=2_K-N._

_Proof._ See Kybalko et al. (2018).

**Theorem 5.3.** _Two optimal Morse flows X,Y are topologically equivalent if and only if_ \(D_X\simeq D_Y\)_, and X is topologically equivalent to the inverse flow_ -_Y if and only if_ \(D_X\simeq D_Y^*\).

_Proof._ See Kybalko et al. (2018).

_Remark_ 5.4. If a one-cycle signed chord diagram _D_ is interpreted as a cellular embedding of a single-vertex graph (a bouquet of _k_ circles) on a closed surface _M_ with a single 2-cell, then the dual chord diagram _D_<sup>∗</sup> specifies the cellular embedding of the topological dual graph _G_<sup>∗</sup> on _M_; _G_<sup>∗</sup> is again a bouquet of _k_ circles with a single 2-cell.

## 6 Software Implementation and Enumeration Data

The enumeration algorithm has been fully implemented in Python and deposited in Zenodo Prishlyak (2026a). For the genus parameter _g_ the program takes _k_=2_g_ and \(\sigma\equiv(+1)^k\) if \(g\ge 0\) (orientable case), and _k_=-_g_ with all 2_<sup>k</sup>_-1 sign vectors different from (+1)_<sup>k</sup>_ if _g\<_0 (non-orientable case).

**Algorithm 2** Enumeration of one-cycle classes

### Validation.

The program was checked against known enumerative results. In the orientable case the number of one-cycle _rooted_ codes equals the Harer-Zagier number \(\varepsilon_g(2g)=\frac{(4g)!}{4^g(2g+1)!}\) Harer and Zagier (1986): 1,21,1485 for _g_=1,2,3. The numbers _N_=1,4,82 of equivalence classes under the dihedral group for _g_=1,2,3 coincide with the numbers of maximal chord diagrams up to all isomorphisms computed by Krasko (2017). For arbitrary sign vectors, the numbers of rooted one-cycle codes (orientable and non-orientable together) 1,5,41,509,8229 for _k_=1_,...,_5 coincide with the numbers of rooted one-vertex one-face maps with _k_ edges on all closed surfaces given there. Moreover, in both cases the sum of the orbit sizes 4_k/_|Stab| over all classes equals the number of rooted one-cycle codes (e.g. 21 for _k_=4 orientable and 41 for _k_=3 non-orientable), and for every class its dual is found in C.

## 7 Conclusion

In this paper, we have established a unified combinatorial framework for the topological classification of optimal Morse flows on closed surfaces based on single-cycle chord diagrams. By leveraging Smale’s theorem, we demonstrated that setting equal values at all saddle critical points naturally translates polar Morse flows into Morse functions corresponding to Fomenko atoms with a single input and output, which map to degree-2 edges on Kronrod-Reeb graphs. The upgraded indexing convention-assigning matching labels \(i\in\{1,\dots,k\}\) to chord endpoints-provides a compact and canonical representation suitable for algorithmic enumeration and dual graph embeddings.

The upgraded indexing convention -- assigning matching labels \(i\in\{1,\dots,k\}\) to chord endpoints -- provides a compact and canonical representation suitable for algorithmic enumeration. Moreover, the dual chord diagram describes the same flow with reversed time: replacing the vector field _X_ by -_X_ interchanges the source and the sink, and the diagram is replaced by its dual. Our algorithm therefore not only lists the diagrams but also finds the pairs of dual diagrams, i.e. the pairs of mutually reversed flows, and the self-dual diagrams, i.e. the flows equivalent to their reverses. For example, among the 82 diagrams of genus _g_=3 there are 30 self-dual ones and 26 dual pairs, so there are 56 classes of flows up to time reversal.

The methodology developed here opens several natural avenues for further research and generalizations:

1. **Multi-cycle chord diagrams:** Extending the canonical chord encoding from single-source (polar) flows to arbitrary Morse-Smale flows with multiple sources and sinks on higher-genus closed surfaces.<tbc>

2. **Manifolds with boundary:** Adapting the chord-diagram formalism to capture boundary critical points, sliding vector fields, and boundary-parallel trajectories on surfaces with non-empty boundary.<tbc>

3. **Higher-dimensional generalizations:** Applying multi-dimensional handle decomposition codes and generalized Reeb graphs to classify Morse-Smale flows on 3-manifolds and 4-manifolds.<tbc>

4. **Software ecosystem and visualization:** Integrating our single-cycle chord diagram algorithms with interactive software packages on Zenodo Prishlyak (2026a,b) to facilitate the automated generation, dual transformation, and visual rendering of complex dynamical phase portraits.<tbc>

## 8 Appendix. Catalog of One-Cycle Chord Diagrams

This section contains a comprehensive graphical atlas of representative one-cycle signed chord diagrams generated for \(g\in\{-5,-4,\dots,3\}\). New figures can be inserted into the template structures below.

### 8.1 From the computational code to the drawing code

For computations a one-cycle chord diagram with _k_ chords is stored as a word _w_=(_w_<sub>1</sub>_,...,w_<sub>2_k_</sub>) in which every label \(m\in\{1,\dots,k\}\) occurs exactly twice (the two ends of chord _m_), together with a sign \(\varepsilon_m\in\{+1,-1\}\) for each chord. The word is normalised by first occurrence, so the labels first appear in the order 1,2_,...,k_. Orientable diagrams (\(g\ge 0\), _k_=2_g_) have all \(\varepsilon_m=+1\); non-orientable ones (_g\<_0, _k_=-_g_) have at least one \(\varepsilon_m=-1\).

The drawing code used by the macro \\cd is a list of triples a/b/c, where _a\<b_ are the cyclic numbers of the ends of a chord on the circle with _n_=2_k_ points, and c is its colour. The conversion is:

1. Number the ends cyclically 1_,...,n_ in the order of the word; position _i_ is drawn at the polar angle \(90^\circ-360^\circ i/n\), i.e. clockwise starting just after the top point.<tbc>

2. For each label _m_ let _a<sub>m</sub>\<b<sub>m</sub>_ be the two positions with _w<sub>a<sub>m</sub></sub>=w<sub>b<sub>m</sub></sub>=m_.<tbc>

3. Put _c<sub>m</sub>_=`B` (blue) if \(\varepsilon_m=+1\) and _c<sub>m</sub>_=`R` (red) if \(\varepsilon_m=-1\).<tbc>

4. Output the triples _a<sub>m</sub>/b<sub>m</sub>/c<sub>m</sub>_ for _m_=1_,...,k_ separated by commas. Because of the normalisation \(a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_k\), no extra sorting is needed.

The diagram is then inserted as \\cd\[s\]{n}{list}, with _n_=2_k_ and scale _s_ (we use 0.62-0.65). For example, the word 12123434 (all signs +1) gives \\cd\[0.62\]{8}{1/3/B,2/4/B,5/7/B,6/8/B}. The empty diagram of the sphere is drawn as \\cd\[0.62\]{2}{}}.

### 8.2 Order, numbering, duality

Within each genus the diagrams are the representatives of the equivalence classes under rotation, reflection and relabelling, one per class: the representative is the lexicographically smallest normalised word in its class, and the classes are listed in increasing order of this word. The number under a diagram is the counter cdn, reset at the start of each genus and continued across figures if the list of one genus does not fit into one figure.

The dual diagram is obtained by traversing the unique face of the diagram: starting at an arc of the circle, we move along the circle to the next chord end, cross the chord to its other end, and continue along the circle in the same direction if the chord is untwisted and in the opposite direction if it is twisted, until we return to the starting arc. The sequence of chords crossed along the way is the word of the dual diagram. The dual chord _m_ is untwisted if the two crossings of chord _m_ go in opposite directions (from its smaller end to its larger one and back), and twisted if both go the same way. The dual is then reduced to its canonical form and found in the same list; a diagram is self-dual if it coincides with its own dual, otherwise it forms a dual pair. After each list we state the numbers of the self-dual diagrams and of the dual pairs.

## Tool use declaration

The enumeration and duality computations were performed with Python programs `one\_cycle\_chord\_diagrams.py` and `general\_codes.py` Prishlyak (2026a,b); the figures were typeset with LATEX and TikZ.

Generative AI (Claude, Anthropropic) was used as follows: (i) writing and debugging parts of the Python code, including the scripts that generate the catalog of chord diagrams in the Appendix (conversion from the computational code to the drawing code, canonical forms, dual and self-dual diagrams); (ii) generating the LATEX/TikZ source of the Appendix figures from the program output; (iii) drafting and editing the English text of the description of the algorithms and of some passages of the Introduction and Conclusion, and suggesting arXiv subject classes.

All mathematical statements, definitions and results come from the authors and from the cited literature. The authors checked the program output independently (for example, by verifying that taking the dual twice returns the original diagram and that the counts of diagrams are consistent with the known ones), reviewed and edited all AI-generated text and code, and take full responsibility for the content of the paper.
